fields.Front: List the defining properties of a weak entity type.
fields.Back:
1. It has NO key attribute of its own
2. It cannot exist without its identifying owner
3. It always has TOTAL participation with the owner (always a double line)
4. The owner's participation may be partial (a building with no rooms recorded)
5. It has a PARTIAL KEY (discriminator) with a dashed underline; full key = owner's key + partial key
6. Drawn as a double rectangle, with a double-diamond identifying relationship
7. It can sometimes be modelled instead as a composite multi-valued attribute of the owner

fields.Front: What are the instructor's two tests for a weak entity?
fields.Back:
1. THE KEY ISN'T REALLY A KEY: it only identifies the entity within some other entity (room 24 exists in Middlesex College and in Natural Sciences; a dependent's name is unique only within one family).
2. CAN IT EXIST WITHOUT THE OTHER ENTITY? 'Can the room exist if the building didn't exist? No.' Her other favourite: a cell cannot exist without the spreadsheet.

fields.Front: In BUILDING HAS ROOM: why is ROOM weak, what is its partial key and its full key, and what is the cardinality?
fields.Back: RoomNumber 'uniquely identifies it within the building, but not to other buildings' - Middlesex College and Natural Sciences may both have a room 110 - and a room cannot exist without its building. Partial key: RoomNumber (dashed underline). Full key: (BuildingCode, RoomNumber). Cardinality: BUILDING (1) HAS (M) ROOM, with BUILDING the identifying owner.

fields.Front: Contrast Student TAKES Course with Building HAS Room using the existence test.
fields.Back: A student can exist without the course and a course without the student - an ordinary relationship between two strong entities. A room cannot exist without its building - so ROOM is weak and BUILDING is its identifying owner.

fields.Front: When could a weak entity be represented instead as an attribute of the owner, and what makes an entity the better choice?
fields.Back: As a COMPOSITE, MULTI-VALUED attribute, e.g. Rooms(RoomNumber, FloorNumber, SquareMetres) on BUILDING - 'that would work too; they're very similar'. Choose a (weak) entity when it has many attributes or relationships of its own: adding TENANT (1) RENTS (M) ROOM makes ROOM better as an entity.

fields.Front: Case study: which entity is weak, who owns it, what is the partial key and what is the participation?
fields.Back: DEPENDENT is weak (double rectangle); owner EMPLOYEE ('the dependent can't exist without the employee'); identifying relationship HAS / DEPENDENTS OF (double diamond), EMPLOYEE (1) to DEPENDENT (N). Partial key: Name (dashed underline); full key after mapping (SSN, Name). Participation: DEPENDENT total (double line), EMPLOYEE partial (single line).

fields.Front: APPLICATION: a hotel database has HOTEL and ROOM, where room numbers restart in each hotel and a room disappears if the hotel does. Model it.
fields.Back: ROOM is a weak entity (double rectangle) owned by HOTEL, with identifying relationship HAS (double diamond), HOTEL (1) to ROOM (N). Partial key RoomNumber (dashed underline); full key (HotelID, RoomNumber). ROOM has total participation (double line); HOTEL may be partial.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §3.5): a DRIVER_LICENSE cannot exist without a PERSON, so why is it NOT a weak entity, and what does that say about the instructor's two tests?
fields.Back:
Because it HAS ITS OWN KEY, License_number. It is existence-dependent but not weak: 'not every existence dependency results in a weak entity type'.
So the two tests are NOT equivalent, and only the first is decisive. Apply them in order:
1. Does it have a key of its own? If yes, it is a STRONG entity, full stop.
2. If not, is it identified through another entity's key combined with one of its own attributes? Then it is WEAK, and that other entity is the owner.
'Cannot exist without the owner' is evidence, not proof.

fields.Text: A weak entity is drawn as a {{c1::double rectangle}}, its identifying relationship as a {{c1::double diamond}}, its partial key with a {{c1::dashed underline}}, and its line to the identifying relationship is always double (total participation).

An identifying owner does {{c1::not}} have to have any weak entities - the owner's participation may be {{c1::partial}} (a building with no rooms recorded) - even though the weak entity's participation is always {{c1::total}}. Contrast: nobody else will ever get her student number, a true key; a room number is not like that.
ROOM is in both HAS and RENTS, but only {{c1::HAS}} gets the double diamond, because the {{c1::building owns}} the room while the tenant merely {{c1::rents}} it.

A dependent's Name is only a {{c1::partial}} key: it is unique {{c1::within one family}}, but another family may also have named their son {{c1::John}}. The standing joke is George Foreman, who named all his sons George - the one family for which even the partial key fails.

Textbook (Elmasri §3.5): the owner entity type is also called the {{c1::parent (or dominant)}} entity type, the weak entity type is also called the {{c1::child (or subordinate)}} entity type, and the partial key is also called the {{c1::discriminator}}. In the worst case the partial key is a composite of all of the weak entity's attributes.
